title: Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization
description: Simplified, qualitative p5.js model of the Aplysia gill-withdrawal reflex. Learners touch the siphon to produce habituation (a shrinking response from a weakening sensory-to-motor synapse), shock the tail to produce sensitization (serotonin from a facilitating interneuron increases transmitter release), and rest the animal to see partial recovery. A bar chart tracks response amplitude across trials and a meter shows synaptic strength.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Explain how repeated siphon touches weaken the sensory-to-motor synapse and produce habituation of the gill-withdrawal reflex.
Explain how serotonin released by a facilitating interneuron after a tail shock strengthens the sensory-to-motor synapse and produces sensitization.
Describe how rest allows partial recovery from short-term habituation.
keyQuestions: Why does the same siphon touch produce a smaller response after many repetitions?
Where in the circuit does the change that causes habituation happen?
How does a shock to the tail change the response to a touch on the siphon?
What does rest do to a habituated reflex?
misconceptions: Habituation is just muscle fatigue or tired sense organs. In Aplysia, the key change is reduced transmitter release at the sensory-to-motor synapse.
Sensitization means the siphon touch itself got stronger. The touch is the same; serotonin makes the sensory neuron release more transmitter.
Learning requires a big brain. A sea slug with a small nervous system shows simple forms of learning.
notes: Response values are arbitrary units chosen to show the direction of change. The model is short-term only and does not show long-term memory, which in Aplysia requires new protein synthesis and growth of synaptic connections.
